{{short description|Number of times an object must be counted for making true a general formula}}
{{wiktionary|multiplicity}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''multiplicity''' of a member of a [[multiset]] is the number of times it appears in the multiset.  For example, the number of times a given [[polynomial]] has a [[Root of a function|root]] at a given point is the multiplicity of that root.

The notion of multiplicity is important to be able to count correctly without specifying exceptions (for example, ''double roots'' counted twice).  Hence the expression, "counted with multiplicity".

If multiplicity is ignored, this may be emphasized by counting the number of ''distinct'' elements, as in "the number of distinct roots". However, whenever a [[set (mathematics)|set]] (as opposed to multiset) is formed, multiplicity is automatically ignored, without requiring use of the term "distinct".

==Multiplicity of a prime factor==
{{main|p-adic valuation}}

In [[Integer factorization|prime factorization]], the '''multiplicity''' of a prime factor is its [[p-adic valuation|<math>p</math>-adic valuation]]. For example, the prime factorization of the [[integer]] {{math|60}} is

: {{math|1=60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5,}}

the multiplicity of the prime factor {{math|2}} is {{math|2}}, while the multiplicity of each of the prime factors {{math|3}} and {{math|5}} is {{math|1}}.  Thus, {{math|60}} has four prime factors allowing for multiplicities, but only three distinct prime factors.

==Multiplicity of a root of a polynomial==
<!-- [[Eigenvalue, eigenvector and eigenspace]] links to this section. Change the link there if you change this header -->

Let <math>F</math> be a [[field (mathematics)|field]] and <math>p(x)</math> be a [[polynomial]] in one variable with [[coefficient]]s in <math>F</math>. An element <math>a \in F</math> is a '''[[root of a function|root]] of multiplicity''' <math>k</math> of <math>p(x)</math> if there is a polynomial <math>s(x)</math> such that <math>s(a)\neq 0</math> and <math>p(x) = (x-a)^k s(x)</math>.  If <math>k=1</math>, then ''a'' is called a '''simple root'''. If <math>k \geq 2</math>, then <math>a</math> is called a '''multiple root'''.

For example, the polynomial <math>p(x) = x^3 + 2x^2 - 7x + 4</math> has 1 and −4 as [[Root of a function|roots]] and can be written as <math>p(x) = (x+4)(x-1)^2</math>, which means that 1 is a root of multiplicity&nbsp;2, and −4 is a simple root (of multiplicity&nbsp;1).  The multiplicity of a root is the number of occurrences of this root in the complete factorization of the polynomial, by means of the [[fundamental theorem of algebra]].

If <math>a</math> is a root of multiplicity <math>k</math> of a polynomial, then it is a root of multiplicity <math>k-1</math> of the [[formal derivative|derivative]] of that polynomial, unless the [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] of the underlying field is a divisor of {{mvar|k}}, in which case <math>a</math> is a root of multiplicity at least <math>k</math> of the derivative.

The [[discriminant]] of a polynomial is zero if and only if the polynomial has a multiple root.

=== Behavior of a polynomial function near a multiple root ===

[[File:Polynomial roots multiplicity.svg|thumb|Graph of ''x''<sup>3</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;2''x''<sup>2</sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;7''x''&nbsp;+&nbsp;4 with a simple root (multiplicity 1) at x=−4 and a root of multiplicity 2 at x=1. The graph crosses the ''x'' axis at the simple root. It is tangent to the ''x'' axis at the multiple root and does not cross it, since the multiplicity is even.|upright]]

The [[graph of a function|graph]] of a [[polynomial function]] ''f'' [[set intersection|intersects]] the ''x''-axis at the real roots of the polynomial. The graph is [[tangent]] to this axis at the multiple roots of ''f'' and not tangent at the simple roots. The graph traverses the ''x''-axis at roots of odd multiplicity and does not traverse it at roots of even multiplicity, where "to traverse the ''x''-axis" means that, near the root, there are points of the graph on both sides of the axis.

A non-zero polynomial function is everywhere [[non-negative]] if and only if all its roots have even multiplicity and there exists an <math>x_0</math> such that <math>f(x_0) > 0</math>.

==Multiplicity of a solution of a nonlinear system of equations==

For an equation <math>f(x)=0</math> with a single variable solution <math>x_*</math>, the multiplicity is <math>k</math> if

:<math>f(x_*)=f'(x_*) = \cdots = f^{(k-1)}(x_*)=0</math> and <math>f^{(k)}(x_*)\neq0.</math>

In other words, the differential functional <math>\partial_j</math>, defined as the derivative <math>\frac{1}{j!}\frac{d^j}{dx^j}</math> of a function at <math>x_*</math>, vanishes at <math>f</math> for <math>j</math> up to <math>k-1</math>. Those differential functionals <math>\partial_0, \partial_1,\cdots,\partial_{k-1}</math> span a [[vector space]], called the '''Macaulay dual space''' at <math>x_*</math>,<ref name="bshw">{{cite book |last1=D.J. Bates, A.J. Sommese, J.D. Hauenstein and C.W. Wampler |title=Numerically Solving Polynomial Systems with Bertini |date=2013 |publisher=SIAM |pages=186–187}}</ref> and its dimension is the multiplicity of <math>x_*</math> as a zero of <math>f</math>.

Let <math>\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{0}</math> be a system of <math>m</math> equations of <math>n</math> variables with a solution <math>\mathbf{x}_*</math> where <math>\mathbf{f}</math> is a mapping from <math>R^n</math> to <math>R^m</math> or from <math>C^n</math> to <math>C^m</math>. There is also a Macaulay dual space of differential functionals at <math>\mathbf{x}_*</math> in which every functional vanishes at <math>\mathbf{f}</math>. The dimension of this Macaulay dual space is the multiplicity of the solution <math>\mathbf{x}_*</math> to the equation <math>\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{0}</math>. The Macaulay dual space forms the multiplicity structure of the system at the solution.<ref name=blz>{{cite journal |last1=B.H. Dayton, T.-Y. Li and Z. Zeng|title=Multiple zeros of nonlinear systems |journal=Mathematics of Computation |date=2011 |volume=80 |issue=276 |pages=2143–2168 |doi=10.1090/s0025-5718-2011-02462-2 |arxiv=2103.05738 |s2cid=9867417 }}</ref><ref name="mac">{{cite book |last1=Macaulay |first1=F.S. |title=The Algebraic Theory of Modular Systems |date=1916 |publisher=Cambridge Univ. Press 1994, reprint of 1916 original}}</ref>

For example, the solution <math>\mathbf{x}_*=(0,0)</math> of the system of equations in the form of  <math>\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{0}</math> with

:<math>\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})=\left[\begin{array}{c} \sin(x_1)-x_2+x_1^2 \\ x_1-\sin(x_2)+x_2^2 \end{array}\right] </math>

is of multiplicity 3 because the Macaulay dual space

:<math> \operatorname{span} \{\partial_{00}, \partial_{10}+\partial_{01}, -\partial_{10}+\partial_{20}+\partial_{11}+\partial_{02}\}</math>

is of dimension 3, where <math>\partial_{ij}</math> denotes the differential functional <math>\frac{1}{i!j!}\frac{\partial^{i+j}}{\partial x_1^i \, \partial x_2^j}</math> applied on a function at the point <math>\mathbf{x}_*=(0,0)</math>.

The multiplicity is always finite if the solution is isolated, is perturbation invariant in the sense that a <math>k</math>-fold solution becomes a cluster of solutions with a combined multiplicity <math>k</math> under perturbation in complex spaces, and is identical to the intersection multiplicity on polynomial systems.

==Intersection multiplicity==
{{main|Intersection multiplicity}}
In [[algebraic geometry]], the intersection of two sub-varieties of an algebraic variety is a finite union of [[irreducible variety|irreducible varieties]]. To each component of such an intersection is attached an ''intersection multiplicity''. This notion is [[local property|local]] in the sense that it may be defined by looking at what occurs in a neighborhood of any [[generic point]] of this component. It follows that [[without loss of generality]], we may consider, in order to define the intersection multiplicity, the intersection of two [[affine variety|affines varieties]] (sub-varieties of an affine space).

Thus, given two affine varieties ''V''<sub>1</sub> and ''V''<sub>2</sub>, consider an [[irreducible component]] ''W'' of the intersection of ''V''<sub>1</sub> and ''V''<sub>2</sub>. Let ''d'' be the [[dimension of an algebraic variety|dimension]] of ''W'', and ''P'' be any generic point of ''W''. The intersection of ''W'' with ''d'' [[hyperplane]]s in [[general position]] passing through ''P'' has an irreducible component that is reduced to the single point ''P''. Therefore, the [[local ring]] at this component of the [[coordinate ring]] of the intersection has only one [[prime ideal]], and is therefore an [[Artinian ring]]. This ring is thus a [[finite dimensional]] vector space over the ground field. Its dimension is the intersection multiplicity of ''V''<sub>1</sub> and ''V''<sub>2</sub> at ''W''.

This definition allows us to state [[Bézout's theorem]] and its generalizations precisely.

This definition generalizes the multiplicity of a root of a polynomial in the following way. The roots of a polynomial ''f'' are points on the [[affine line]], which are the components of the algebraic set defined by the polynomial. The coordinate ring of this affine set is <math>R=K[X]/\langle f\rangle, </math> where ''K'' is an [[algebraically closed field]] containing the coefficients of ''f''. If <math>f(X)=\prod_{i=1}^k (X-\alpha_i)^{m_i}</math> is the factorization of ''f'', then the local ring of ''R'' at the prime ideal <math>\langle X-\alpha_i\rangle</math> is <math>K[X]/\langle (X-\alpha)^{m_i}\rangle.</math> This is a vector space over ''K'', which has the multiplicity <math>m_i</math> of the root as a dimension.

This definition of intersection multiplicity, which is essentially due to [[Jean-Pierre Serre]] in his book ''Local Algebra'', works only for the set theoretic components (also called ''isolated components'') of the intersection, not for the [[embedded prime|embedded components]]. Theories have been developed for handling the embedded case (see [[Intersection theory]] for details).

==In complex analysis==
Let ''z''<sub>0</sub> be a root of a [[holomorphic function]] ''f'', and let ''n'' be the least positive integer such that the ''n''<sup>th</sup> derivative of ''f'' evaluated at ''z''<sub>0</sub> differs from zero. Then the [[power series]] of ''f'' about ''z''<sub>0</sub> begins with the ''n''<sup>th</sup> term, and ''f'' is said to have a root of multiplicity (or "order")&nbsp;''n''. If ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1, the root is called a simple root.<ref>(Krantz 1999, p.&nbsp;70)</ref>

We can also define the multiplicity of the [[Zero (complex analysis)|zeroes]] and [[Pole (complex analysis)|poles]] of a [[meromorphic function]]. If we have a meromorphic function <math display="inline">f = \frac{g}{h},</math> take the [[Taylor series|Taylor expansions]] of ''g'' and ''h'' about a point ''z''<sub>0</sub>, and find the first non-zero term in each (denote the order of the terms ''m'' and ''n'' respectively) then if ''m''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''n'', then the point has non-zero value. If <math>m>n,</math> then the point is a zero of multiplicity <math>m-n.</math> If <math>m<n</math>, then the point has a pole of multiplicity <math>n-m.</math> The [[argument principle]] counts zeroes and poles according to their multiplicity.
